Describing Student Growth

Measuring student growth, even with a vertical scale, is not a
simple task.
Even with an interval (or ratio) scale, growth is not easy to
interpret. Consider, for example, height.
A child might grow 4 inches between ages 3 and 4.
4 inches is a well understood quantity.
The 4 inch increase becomes really meaningful only when
understood alongside the growth of other 3 to 4 year olds.
Student growth percentiles were developed to provide a
normative context for describing student growth.

Normative Growth Model
Should we be surprised with a child’s current achievement given
their prior achievement?

Pr(Current Achievement |Past Achievement ).

Quantile regression is used to model the conditional quantile
functions.
B-spline smoothing is applied to accommodate non-linearity,
heteroscedasticity, etc. Scatterplot Smoothing
The method is a quantile regression based generalized
additive model [Hastie and Tibshirani, 1990, Wood, 2006]
Implemented in R using SGP Package

Normative and Criterion-Referenced Growth

“Adequate” Growth: Is a student’s (normative) growth sufficient to
reach/maintain desired performance standards (e.g., proficiency)?

Norms are blind to standards? Equally rare does not imply
equally good.
Using the coefficient matrices from the quantile regression
analyses, percentile growth projections/trajectories are
calculated for each student.
These “growth-to-standard” trajectories indicate what it will
take for the student to reach/maintain proficiency and other
performance standards.
The Colorado Growth Model was recently approved as part of
the Growth Model Pilot Program using this approach.

An even bigger picture

The education system, being composed of students, can be
examined similarly.
Using performance on annual student assessments, consider
an entire education system over time.
Standards and norm referenced interpretations are necessary
to grasp the performance of the system in it’s entirety.
Looked at appropriately, there is a beautiful (and predictable)
interplay between norms and standards.

Conclusions

Norm shouldn’t be a four letter word.
Performance standards across grades that are (normatively)
(dis)similar will lead to (un)reasonable growth trajectories.
A “growth model” anchored to standards will not save you
from uneven standards.
Normative effectiveness models (value-added models) are
blind to standards (so they save you in that respect)

Conclusions

If resetting standards or transitioning to a new assessment,
having growth data prior to standard setting will probably be
helpful.
Normative growth data would give a sense of what current
student progress currently looks like.
The goal is to balance what is, what should be, and what is
reasonable.
Once that’s in place, productive discussions about
responsibility/accountability can ensue.
